newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FOCUS-Analysts say Hungary C/A, budget on track.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Analysts say Hungary C/A, budget on track.

text.p: Hungary's April current account and June budget data, published on Tuesday, indicate that 1997 figures are likely to be within target levels, analysts said.
"I think the situation is very good," said Zoltan Bereczki of New York Broker.

Figures from the National Bank of Hungary showed that the current account deficit was $110 million in April, producing a gap for the first four months of the year of $587 million, down from $748 million in the same period of 1996.

Gabor Oblath, researcher at independent think-tank Kopint-Datorg, said household consumption and investments began to pick up this year and this could quicken the rate of increase in the deficit in the second half of the year.
Bereczki said the abolition of a three percent import surcharge from July 1 might also increase imports but tourism revenues would also rise in the summer.
Most analysts said that they had not changed their earlier deficit forecasts for 1997, adding they were optimistic that the government would meet a $2 billion target.
In a recent Reuters survey, 13 analysts' forecasts of the 1997 current account deficit averaged $2.1 billion.
Analysts said the April figures showed that despite a recovery in the economy, Hungary did not face current account problems, unlike the Czech Republic and Poland.
This was indicated by the fact that the trade gap widened by $204 million but other items such as tourist revenues improved the current account, they said.
"Tourism revenues really helped the current account," said Robert Rethy of K&H Securities.
Revenues from tourism totalled $281 million in January-April, up from $194 million in the same period of 1996.
However, continued high real wage levels might jeopardise the current account target, Rethy said, triggering a rise in household consumption and boosting imports.
Average real wages rose by 7.2 percent in the January-April period on a year-on-year basis.
"As the (1998) elections are approaching, obviously this is the most sensitive point," Rethy said, adding that the government should not try to win votes by allowing wages to rise too much.
The government targets a real wage rise of about two percent for this year.

Analysts said the June central state budget deficit of 165 billion forints ($873 million), up by 15 billion from May, indicated that Hungary was likely to keep the deficit within the 360 billion target for the year and also meet the general government budget deficit target of 4.9 percent of the gross domestic product.
The June figure was lower than the 171.5 billion forint average of the forecasts of 10 analysts in a recent Reuters survey.
However, analysts said a soaring social security deficit might threaten Hungary's longer-term plans to reduce inflation and boost economic growth at the same time.
Rethy said central bank president Gyorgy Suranyi had been right to stress the point last week at a news conference.
"This is a serious problem. The deficit was very high last year and nothing seems to have changed," he said.
"The impact of this can be offset by other systems in the budget for the moment but a 50 to 60 billion forints gap will remain for the long term."

The International Monetary Fund, the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development and the National Bank of Hungary have all warned recently that the country needs to tackle the high social security deficit.
-- Budapest newsroom (36 1) 327 4040 ($ = 188.9 Hungarian Forints)
